Senses.Explanation: In Chan exchanges, this verb means to miss what is immediately before one or let the moment slip past. Masters turn that ordinary failure into a rapid public answer, verdict, and warning: even raising the eyebrows may already be too late. Kaiyuan Zhizi says that merely raising the eyebrows is already to have missed it (眨上眉毛，早是蹉過). Huguo Cian Jingyuan answers a question about whether there is any further matter with, ‘You missed it face-to-face’ (向上還有事也無？師曰：當面蹉過). Tianyin Yuanxiu warns against missing it face-to-face and adds that, after missing it, one knows only affairs passing before the eyes (切不得當面蹉過；若蹉過，只知事逐眼前過). Baozi Chun uses the same face-to-face answer when asked why it is under the questioner's heel (因甚在汝脚跟下？師曰：當面蹉過). Feiyin Tongrong gives the completed-form verdict, ‘You have missed it’ (蹉過了也), and his interlocutor immediately answers. Yichu Yuan also uses the verb in an admonition not to miss anything in daily activity. These are grammatical and situational variants of one event, not different referents.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. The fixed face-to-face form occurs 158 times in 65 texts, and the completed form occurs 117 times. The Zen-specific bend is observable in its use as a rapid answer, verdict, and admonition in public exchanges; the records do not assign the verb a second lexical object.
